slot.topic_title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

item.title: Claims About a Difference in Mean Reading Fluency
item.stimulus: A school district randomly assigned 40 students to a reading-fluency program and 38 students to a comparison group, and measured each student's reading fluency in words per minute at the end of the term. Program group: mean 61.2, standard deviation 10.4. Comparison group: mean 56.0, standard deviation 9.1. Using technology, an analyst found a 95% confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂, the difference (program minus comparison) in population means, of (0.80, 9.60) words per minute.

criteria.text: Interprets the interval: we are 95% confident that the interval from 0.80 to 9.60 words per minute captures the true difference (program group minus comparison group) in mean reading fluency for all students like these.
criteria.evidence: Response states the confidence level, the interval from 0.80 to 9.60 words per minute, and the parameter it captures (true difference (program group minus comparison group) in mean reading fluency for all students like these).
criteria.fix: Say 'confident the interval captures the true parameter', give the interval and confidence level, and name the parameter in context.

parts.prompt: The program director claims that the program does not change mean reading fluency, that is, that μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Does the interval provide convincing evidence against this claim? Explain.

criteria.text: Because 0 is not in the interval (0.80, 9.60), 0 is not a plausible value of the difference in population means, so the interval provides convincing evidence that the means differ (the program is associated with a difference in mean reading fluency).
criteria.evidence: Response compares 0 with the interval and concludes: 0 is not a plausible value of the difference in population means, so the interval provides convincing evidence that the means differ (the program is associated with a difference in mean reading fluency).
criteria.fix: Check whether the claimed value lies inside the interval: a value outside it is not a plausible value of the parameter.

parts.prompt: The program director also claims that the program raises mean reading fluency by at least 10 words per minute, that is, that μ₁ − μ₂ is at least 10 words per minute. Does the interval support this claim? Explain.

criteria.text: Because 10 is above the interval (0.80, 9.60), 10 is not a plausible value of μ₁ − μ₂ and every plausible value is below it, so the interval does not support the claim.
criteria.evidence: Response compares 10 with the interval and concludes: 10 is not a plausible value of μ₁ − μ₂ and every plausible value is below it, so the interval does not support the claim.
criteria.fix: Check whether the claimed value lies inside the interval: a value outside it is not a plausible value of the parameter.

parts.prompt: Without recalculating, how would a 99% interval from the same data compare in width with this 95% interval? Explain.

criteria.text: States that a 99% interval from the same data would be wider, because a higher confidence level needs a larger critical value t* (a larger margin of error) to capture the parameter more often.
criteria.evidence: Response says the interval would be wider and gives the higher confidence level (larger t*, larger margin of error, capturing the parameter more often) as the reason.
criteria.fix: Hold the standard error fixed: higher confidence means a larger t*, so a larger margin of error and a wider interval.

item.model_answer:
(a) We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.80 to 9.60 words per minute captures the true difference (program group minus comparison group) in mean reading fluency for all students like these.

(b) Yes. Because 0 is not in the interval (0.80, 9.60), it is not a plausible value of μ₁ − μ₂, so the interval provides convincing evidence that the means differ (the program is associated with a difference in mean reading fluency).

(c) No. 10 is above the interval (0.80, 9.60), so it is not a plausible value and every plausible value is below it; the interval does not support the claim.

(d) A 99% interval would be wider, because a higher confidence level uses a larger critical value t*, which increases the margin of error.
